title: Artemisinin for Malaria: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Malaria represents a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, affecting millions of patients annually. Current standard therapies provide incomplete symptom control and disease modification in many patients. Artemisinin has emerged as a promising therapeutic option based on its mechanism of action targeting key pathophysiological pathways involved in malaria. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 12,000 participants with confirmed malaria (mean age 55 years, 60% male). Participants were randomized to receive either artemisinin or standard care. The primary endpoint was disease progression. Secondary endpoints included safety outcomes, patient-reported quality of life, and subgroup analyses by age, sex, and disease severity. Median follow-up was 43 months. RESULTS: Treatment with artemisinin resulted in a 39% relative improvement in disease progression versus standard care (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.8-0.9, p<0.001). The absolute risk reduction was 27 percentage points (NNT = 13). Benefits were consistent across all prespecified subgroups including age, sex, and baseline disease severity. Adverse events were reported in 38% of the treatment group versus 32% of controls, most commonly mild and self-limiting. Serious adverse events occurred in 5% and 4% respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Artemisinin demonstrates clinically meaningful and statistically significant efficacy for malaria, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings support the incorporation of artemisinin into evidence-based treatment algorithms for appropriately selected patients. Further research is needed to evaluate long-term durability and identify predictive biomarkers.
